identity_evidence.quote: This case report describes the 23-year follow-up of a male patient with a history of orthotopic heart transplantation
A 42-year-old Caucasian male, employed as an office worker

attribution_limitations: Whether the gingival overgrowth is drug-induced by cyclosporine: the case text says the condition was consistent with DIGO, most likely related to cyclosporine use, while the abstract and discussion state that DIGO developed under cyclosporine therapy

Course of the overgrowth in 2025: the Figure 5 and 8 captions and the text describe persistent or worsened hypertrophy and inflammation, while the Figure 6 caption describes regression of overgrowth in selected papillary regions and the conclusions describe alternating phases of regression and recurrence
Which sample the RT-PCR for Candida was run on is not stated

The text says maintenance was discontinued for approximately three years and also that the patient was followed for 23 years with maintenance for more than two decades; the interval between return of care and the sampling visit is not stated beyond the 2025 follow-up visit
The authors state that the abstract transplant timing is two years before the first visit in 2002, while the case text gives late 1999; the two are consistent only approximately
The authors' statement that interruption of supportive periodontal care may have contributed to biofilm re-accumulation and deterioration is an interpretation

The per-taxon abundance values are stated in the case text, which gives no collection time; the 2025 follow-up timing is stated only in the Figure 9 and 10 caption leads and in the discussion (At the 23-year follow-up), so it is carried on the sampling, assessment and profile items and on the sampling event, not on each taxon item

evidence.quote:
Figure 1
Intraoral photography from the patient's initial clinical examination in 2002, showing the right maxillary and mandibular hemi-arches with marked hypertrophy of the interdental papillae (white arrows).

Figure 2
Intraoral photography from the patient's initial clinical examination in 2002, showing the left maxillary and mandibular hemi-arches with marked hypertrophy of the interdental papillae (white arrows).

Figure 3
Intraoral frontal view from the patient's initial clinical examination in 2002, showing hypertrophic interdental papillae (white arrows) and the presence of an unaesthetic prosthetic crown on the upper right central incisor (yellow arrow), contributing to the compromised gingival architecture and an overall unaesthetic smile.

Figure 4
An intraoral view captured a few months after the patient's initial clinical examination in 2002, showing the newly restored maxillary right central incisor (yellow arrow) and the hypertrophic interdental papilla between the two central incisors (white arrow), still present despite the patient's hygiene efforts and regular follow-up appointments.

Figure 5
Intraoral photography (right lateral view) taken in 2025, showing lobulated gingival overgrowth with persistent hypertrophy of the interdental papillae and signs of inflammation (white arrows), consistent with disease progression in the absence of regular periodontal maintenance.

Figure 6
Intraoral photography (left lateral view) captured in 2025 reveals a clear regression of gingival overgrowth in selected papillary regions (white arrows), compared to images taken 23 years earlier. Despite this improvement, notable plaque accumulation persists on the posterior teeth, accompanied by bleeding on probing, periodontal pocket depths up to 5 mm, and clinical attachment loss ranging from 3 to 4 mm in specific sites.

Figure 7
Intraoral frontal view captured in 2025, highlighting the flaring (splaying) of the maxillary central incisors (yellow arrows) and the presence of inflamed, hypertrophic papillary tissue (white arrow) between the central incisors.

Figure 8
An intraoral frontal view captured in 2025 reveals flaring (splaying) of the maxillary central incisors (yellow arrows), inflamed and hypertrophic papillary tissue between the central incisors (white arrow), purulent exudate along the gingival margin, and generalized tooth discoloration with darker shades affecting the dentition.

Figure 9
Relative abundance of bacterial taxa identified in the subgingival plaque sample from the maxillary central incisors pocket, collected during the 2025 follow-up visit, revealing a dysbiotic microbial profile. The red-colored slice represents the relative abundance of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a keystone pathogen implicated in the onset and progression of periodontal disease. Of particular note, the detection of Fusobacterium nucleatum highlights its ecological role as a bridging organism contributing to subgingival biofilm maturation and dysbiosis.Figure created by the authors using open-source software (Python/matplotlib).

Figure 10
Relative abundance of bacterial taxa identified in the tongue dorsum sample, collected during the 2025 follow-up visit, showing a microbial composition consistent with relative eubiosis.Figure created by the authors using open-source software (Python/matplotlib).
